articles.title: “He won’t retire from life”: Inside Roger Federer’s $300M Uniqlo deal and the ‘billionaire’ twist behind his fortune
articles.summary: International Sports News: Roger Federer’s biggest financial wins did not come from tennis tournaments. The 20-time Grand Slam champion earned nearly $131 million in ATP prize m.
articles.body: Roger Federer’s biggest financial wins did not come from tennis tournaments. The 20-time Grand Slam champion earned nearly $131 million in ATP prize money during his career, but his wealth grew much faster through major brand deals and investments. His 2018 move from Nike to Uniqlo gave him a reported $300 million deal over 10 years, while his 2019 investment in Swiss sportswear company On became even more valuable. Forbes estimated Federer’s fortune at $1.1 billion in March 2026, but a sharp fall in On shares later pushed it below $1 billion.Roger Federer’s $300 million Uniqlo deal after leaving NikeFederer’s first major move came in 2018, when he ended his long relationship with Nike and joined Uniqlo. The reported deal was worth $300 million over 10 years, or about $30 million a year. More importantly, it was not tied to how long Federer would continue playing tennis.That mattered because Federer was already 36 when he signed the deal. Uniqlo was buying into his wider appeal, not just his results on the court. The thinking behind the partnership was summed up by a senior Uniqlo creative executive, who said: “Roger will retire from tennis, but he won’t retire from life.”Federer later explained the idea himself in a Uniqlo interview: “I might retire from tennis at some point, but not from life. UNIQLO understands that about me. After all, it’s more than just a clothing company. It’s a lifestyle. That’s what makes it LifeWear.”The deal also left Federer free to find a separate footwear partner because Uniqlo does not make tennis shoes. That opened the door to the investment that changed the value of his business portfolio.Roger Federer turned his On investment into a major fortuneIn 2019, Federer became an investor and co-entrepreneur with Swiss sportswear company On. He reportedly put about $50 million into the company for an estimated 3% stake. The exact terms were not publicly disclosed by On, but the reported investment has become one of the most valuable deals made by an athlete.Federer was not simply paid to wear the shoes. He worked with On on products, including The Roger line, giving him a role in the business as well as a stake in it.On went public on the New York Stock Exchange in 2021 at a valuation of about $11 billion. Federer’s stake was then worth hundreds of millions of dollars. In 2026, recent estimates put the value of his On holding at around $310 million after a major fall in the company’s share price.That fall also shows why Federer’s net worth can change quickly. Forbes reported in August 2026 that his fortune dropped to about $952.4 million after On shares plunged following weaker-than-expected results. So while Federer reached billionaire status in recent estimates, his wealth is closely tied to the value of his On stake.Roger Federer’s foundation has put millions into educationFederer has also directed a large part of his money and time toward education. He started the Roger Federer Foundation with his parents in 2003, when he was 22. The foundation focuses mainly on early and basic education in Southern Africa and Switzerland.By the end of 2024, the foundation said it had spent 95 million Swiss francs and helped improve the quality of education at 17,531 educational institutions. More than 3.1 million children had benefited from its work.The work is closely linked to Federer’s focus on giving young children a stronger start in school. During his work with the foundation, he said: “Early education is the foundation of learning.”That makes his post-tennis story different from a simple list of endorsement deals. Federer earned most of his playing income on the court, but his biggest financial gains came from choosing long-term partnerships and ownership. At the same time, his foundation has put tens of millions into education, giving another side to the wealth he built after becoming one of tennis’ biggest stars.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: Bayley made her return to WWE Raw on Monday night to get revenge on Lyra Valkyria after being off television for nearly two months following Lyra's post-match attack at WWE Saturday Night's Main Event in July.
articles.body:
Bayley made her return to WWE Raw on Monday night to get revenge on Lyra Valkyria after being off television for nearly two months following Lyra's post-match attack at WWE Saturday Night's Main Event in July.

Sol Ruca pinned Lyra after Bayley's distraction to qualify for Money in the Bank, eliminating Lyra's chances for the ladder match, unless there's a last-chance qualifier in the future.

Given the brutal attack in July, Bayley vs. Lyra would be a strong undercard match for the WWE Money in the Bank PLE on Oct. 10 in New Orleans.

During Bayley's hiatus, rumors swirled surrounding her contract status and future with WWE. False Finish reported on Sept. 3 that Bayley "re-signed and will be more involved with the company and not just as an on screen talent."

A future hall of famer, Bayley's return is a major boost for Raw's women's division. After she concludes her rivalry with Lyra, it would only make sense for Bayley to be pushed into the title picture with Liv Morgan, Stephanie Vaquer and Becky Lynch.

articles.title: 'That was a pity': Viswanathan Anand after losing on time to Magnus Carlsen, who lauds India's 'love for chess'
articles.summary: Chess News: BENGALURU: The fast-paced world of chess has seen many terms evolve over time. “Flagging” is one of them. It generally refers to winning a game purely.
articles.body: BENGALURU: The fast-paced world of chess has seen many terms evolve over time. “Flagging” is one of them. It generally refers to winning a game purely on time when an opponent’s clock hits 0:00, regardless of the evaluation on the board. From the perspective of both players and spectators, it’s a tense, chaotic climax where speed outruns strategy.On Monday, that exact high-wire drama took centre stage during the Day 3 marquee clash between APL Pipers' Magnus Carlsen and Alaskan Knights' Viswanathan Anand on the icon board. With seconds ticking down in a sharp middle-game battle, Anand failed to hit his clock in time, allowing Carlsen to snatch a win on time."A few moves ago, I had a few seconds more than him, so somehow my brain stopped looking at the clock, and I didn't keep one second left,” Anand told reporters after the opening match of the day. "Once I make a move, I will get some time, but apparently I let my clock run out. That was a pity, but I'm happy the team won."Despite losing his game, Anand’s squad pulled off the overall match victory. "I'm not happy with my play, but at least it didn't cost us," the five-time world champion added.The current World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen also gave his side of the dramatic finish against his longtime rival."I felt like I was playing him a little bit in the middle game. I was pretty happy with the position from the opening, and then again I was a little bit shaky with little time,” Carlsen stated.“For a period there, he was defending very, very well, not making it any worse, and then I just obviously resigned myself to a draw. Then I randomly glanced at his clock and saw that it was out. That's how it goes sometimes at times like this."Later, in Pipers’ game against the Gambits, Carlsen also raised eyebrows by uncorking 3...f6 against World Championship challenger Javokhir Sindarov, before holding him to a draw.Explaining the unexpected move, Carlsen added, "It (the idea) was originally from my coach. It was a misclick, and then he started looking at it. I kind of like the general idea of taking kind of a random move in the opening, and then with computer analysis, you can make pretty much anything work. The main idea is that after castles, a6, it's actually already not terrible."Despite his self-described "underwhelming" form, Carlsen expressed deep appreciation for the crowd in Bengaluru, saying, "It's very nice to play here. Chess in India is massive. That's great to see, and I definitely want to come here and experience the love people have for chess."What happened on Day 3 in GCL Day 3 saw intense action across four team face-offs. Alaskan Knights edged past Alpine APL Pipers 9–7 in the first match of the day, but the Pipers stormed back later in with a commanding, one-sided 15–3 win over American Gambits. Meanwhile, Mumba Masters dominated Ganges Grandmasters 12–3, while Triveni Continental Kings secured an 11–6 victory, their first in the tournament, over Alaskan Knights in the final match of the day.Following the Day 3 results, APL Pipers hold top spot with 9 match points, closely followed by Mumba Masters, American Gambits, and Alaskan Knights tied at 6 points each. articles.title: In attack mode: Satwik-Chirag train their eyes on Asian Games
articles.summary: Badminton News: A day after becoming the first Indian pair to win the China Masters title, Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty have now trained their sights on .
articles.body: A day after becoming the first Indian pair to win the China Masters title, Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty have now trained their sights on the Asian Games, where they defend the men's doubles gold they won in 2023.The duo remain the only Indian shuttlers to have won gold at the Asian Games, but Chirag insists there is no added pressure to repeat that feat. "We want to go out there and do what we normally do on court. If we're able to do that, I think we'll go deep into the tournament, and that's the only thing we want," said Chirag during a virtual interaction arranged by the Badminton Association of India (BAI) on Monday."We don't want to think too much about the results. When we keep the results aside and take one match at a time, that's when we play our best."The Indians head into the Continental Games in ominous form, riding on their stirring victory in Shenzhen.Chirag believes the pair's biggest challenges will come from two contrasting styles. He rated Korea's Kim Won Ho and Seo Seung Jae as the best defensive combination on the circuit, while world champions Liang Wei Keng and Wang Chang of China remain the most potent attacking pair, albeit a notch below the Indians."Apart from us, I think Liang and Wang are the best attacking players. When it comes to defence, it's Kim Won Ho and Seo Seung Jae," Chirag said.He also acknowledged that his own defensive game still has room for improvement."I've added a few new aspects to my defence, but there's still a lot to be done," he said.Kim and Seo, who won 11 titles last year, began 2026 in equally dominant fashion, claiming three successive titles before Satwik and Chirag ended their streak with a semifinal victory at the Singapore Open on May 31.Since then, the Korean world No. 1 pair has endured a lean spell, failing to win a title in their next six tournaments. Their slump also included a first round exit at the China Masters, where the Indians went on to lift the trophy.For Satwik and Chirag, however, the blueprint remains unchanged. Even if their trademark attacking game is neutralised, Satwik says there is no alternative approach. "It's always Plan A - there's no Plan B for us. But it depends on the opponents. It's never easy. They don't want to lift the shuttle to us either," he said. "Whether it's the Malaysians, Indonesians or even the Chinese, everyone wants to play fast and get into the attack rather than give us a target."Satwik also underlined the importance of Chirag's presence at the front of the court, saying his partner's ability to create openings has made his finishing role considerably easier. "Chirag makes my job so much easier - he creates so many chances for me to finish," he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Steelers HC Mike McCarthy Gives Fresh Update on Joey Porter Jr.’s Contract Talks
articles.summary: One thing that has hovered over the Steelers heading into the offseason and preseason is Joey Porter Jr.’s contract talks, and now that Week 1 of the regular...
articles.body:
One thing that has hovered over the Steelers heading into the offseason and preseason is Joey Porter Jr.'s contract talks, and now that Week 1 of the regular season is here, there is still no resolution.

Porter is entering the final year of his rookie contract. Head coach Mike McCarthy told reporters on Monday that there are "definitely business conversations going on," via ESPN's Brooke Pryor.

Porter has less than six days to sign a new contract. The Steelers have a policy of not negotiating new deals with players, coaches and staff during the regular season.

"We won't talk publicly about the negotiations, but Joey knows how we feel about him, and I still hope Joey finishes his career here," Steelers general manager Omar Khan said in late August. "Our policy is going to remain in place, but I'm not going to talk about negotiations."

Porter Might Not Take the Field on Sunday

When the Steelers take the field for their first game on Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons , there is a good chance that Porter will not be on the field if a new contract isn't reached. He told the media on Tuesday that he may not play with a new contract.

"I don't know; I've got to talk to the guys upstairs, my agents, about that one," Porter said about whether he will play if a deal doesn't get done.

Even though Porter doesn't know if he will play on Sunday, McCarthy said the Steelers are healthy, and there's no one he expects to have trouble playing, including Porter, via Nick Farabaugh.

Porter isn't just dealing with a contract problem; he is also facing an injury issue. He hurt his back on the first day of training camp and missed the entire season.

The Steelers placed him on the PUP list after he hurt his back but took him off it on the final day of roster cuts so he wouldn't have to miss the first four games of the season.

If the Steelers cannot reach a deal with Porter, they may consider trading him during the regular season before he hits free agency next offseason.

Steelers Know Which QB They Will Face in Week 1

While the Steelers don't know whether Porter will play on Sunday, they finally know who the Falcons will start at quarterback.

Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski confirmed that Tua Tagovailoa will start, with Michael Penix Jr. still recovering from a torn ACL suffered last season.

Tagovailoa played six seasons for the Miami Dolphins , finishing his last season appearing in 14 games, recording 2,660 yards and 20 touchdowns. He has a one-and-one record against the Steelers in his career.

The Falcons were close to making the playoffs last season, finishing 8-9. But now, with Stefanski as head coach, they could have a shot at winning the NFC South this season, and it could start with them knocking off the Steelers in Week 1.

articles.title: Shohei Ohtani’s return inspires little confidence as he struggles in Dodgers win
articles.summary: Suddenly, there’s an uncomfortable irony to Shohei Ohtani’s walk-up music. Every time the dulcet tones of Michael Buble singing “…and I’m feeling good” come...
articles.body:
Suddenly, there's an uncomfortable irony to Shohei Ohtani's walk-up music.

Every time the dulcet tones of Michael Buble singing " …and I'm feeling good" come on, the Dodgers have to hope their two-way star does too.

For the first time in almost a week on Monday, Ohtani was feeling good enough to return to the Dodgers' lineup , ending a streak of four-straight games missed previously while he was managing injuries to his right arm and left knee.

However, whatever was ailing him at the plate before his recent absence –– when he went 6-for-46 over a 12-game stretch from Aug. 19 to Sept. 2 –– had clearly yet to be resolved.

While the Dodgers rode another big night from Teoscar Hernández (two hits, including a three-run home run, plus a walk) to a 6-3 defeat of the Cincinnati Reds , Ohtani went 0-for-3 with two strikeouts while drawing only a seventh-inning walk; inspiring little confidence that, even if he's able to take the field right now, his swing is close to being where he would like it to be.

Back in his customary leadoff spot, Ohtani began the night with relatively loud contact, lifting a deep fly ball to left field that died just shy of the warning track.

But after that, the 32-year-old looked largely unchanged from his recent offensive struggles.

He swung through a changeup and slider from young Reds ace Chase Burnes in the third inning, going down on the latter while chasing a pitch in the dirt.

He went down swinging again during his highest-leverage at-bat in the fifth, leaving a runner stranded at third after fanning on a first-pitch sweeper from left-handed reliever Brandon Williamson then whiffing on a two-strike changeup that was at the knees.

Ohtani did show better plate discipline in the seventh, fouling off two pitches in the zone while taking four misses from Williamson for a walk. But even then, he didn't seem completely right –– at one point even appearing to circle his troublesome right arm after a swing (though, it wasn't clear if that was necessarily a sign of pain).

Just like the last four nights, in which the Dodgers all won with Ohtani out of the lineup , the team overcame his lack of impact again to run their winning streak to five games.

Emmet Sheehan was key to that, returning from triple-A Oklahoma City for a 5 ⅔-inning, one-run, 10-strikeout gem.

So too was Hernández, who continued his recent tear by lacing a 112 mph line drive into the left-field bullpen for a three-run homer in the sixth.

An inning before that, a two-run throwing error by Reds' third baseman Ke'Bryan Hayes had also given the Dodgers a lead.

Still, come October, the Dodgers know they will need more from Ohtani at the plate.

That's what has made this last week so tricky, as they tried to balance his tenuous health with the need to give him a chance to rectify his swing.

On Monday, he received a reminder of how much work is left to go –– feeling good enough to return to the field, but not to snap a drought that continues to raise questions about his uncertain health status.

articles.title: Red light turned green; all systems go for Emmet Sheehan
articles.summary: In a battle of strikeouts and power, the Dodgers outmuscle the Reds thanks to a Teoscar Hernández’s three-run home run
articles.body:
Based on tonight's game alone, you could've fooled someone into believing Emmet Sheehan was the starting pitcher in this outing, putting up an All-Star season, as he led the way for a 6-3 win in his return to the bigs. With a scarcity of hits, particularly on the home side, the Dodgers saved their only home run for the most impactful of moments as Teoscar Hernández crushed a three-run bomb in the sixth, responsible for half their runs.

The Reds came into this game with a plan to keep Chase Burns on a tight leash, protecting their prized pitching asset down the stretch in a season without a postseason chase. The game tested the Reds' resolve, with Burns smoking through the Dodgers' lineup in three near-perfect innings—the only Dodger to get on base was Max Muncy via walk. Striking out half of the 10 batters he faced, Burns was still removed from the game after just three frames, paving the way for Brandon Williamson to operate against a lefty-heavy lineup.

Williamson picked up right where Burns left off, and a bit of luck and the right timing helped the Dodgers get on the board for the first time and, doing so, take the lead. Trailing 1-0 through the first half of this game after Elly De La Cruz's first-inning bomb, the Dodgers had one on and two outs in the fifth, following strikeouts from Kyle Tucker and Hunter Feduccia. Alex Call was down 0-2 in the count, ready to make it three Ks when he was plunked by Williamson, who would induce a high-bouncing grounder by Miguel Rojas—that grounder rushed an errant throw from the Reds' third baseman, allowing both runners to score.

As quickly as the Dodgers took that lead, they nearly surrendered it, with the Reds circling in the top of the sixth. Emmet Sheehan faced runners at the corners with one out and the Reds' top two hitters up. He struck out De La Cruz, chasing well outside the zone, to reach a double-digit punchout total—tying a career high—before walking Sal Stewart to load the bases and seal his exit. With a lefty coming up, Dave Roberts made the call to the bullpen, bringing in Alex Vesia, who promptly struck out J.J. Bleday. No pitcher ever wants to hand off a free pass, but as far as they go, the one to Stewart wasn't too bad from Sheehan, not giving up against the league leader in RBI.

Baseball has a term for a scoreless frame right after getting on the board: your traditional shutdown inning, the case for the Dodgers in the top of the sixth. It should also have a term for pouncing on that opportunity and scoring big in the next chance, something like an opportunistic inning , exactly what the Dodgers had in the bottom of the sixth. Max Muncy and Freddie Freeman worked walks off Williamson, and then the lefty-mashing skill set of Teoscar Hernández took over, putting one in the home bullpen over the left field wall to up the lead to 5-1.

This power display from Hernández was the perfect summary of a heavy three-true-outcome game, one in which both teams combined for an absurd 20 strikeouts in the first six innings alone. Emmet Sheehan (10), Chase Burns (5), Brandon Williamson (4)—basically anyone was able to induce swing-and-miss stuff consistently. Furthermore, when Eugenio Suárez took Seth Halvorsen deep for the Reds' second solo shot to make it 5-2 in the seventh, half of the game's six hits were home runs. What put the Dodgers in front was superior defense and an easier ability to draw walks.

The Reds don't get to lament their lack of opportunities in this one. Pitching in the eighth, Jack Dreyer faced two on and no one out, defending a three-run lead with the heart of the Reds' order up. Operating like someone leading by three, Dreyer punched out Stewart and allowed an RBI groundout to pinch-hitter Dane Myers, replacing Bleday, whom Terry Francona wouldn't allow to have another lefty-lefty duel late in this game. Whatever impact that run might have had was neutralized when Will Smith pinch-hit with the bases loaded in the bottom of the frame and secured a sac fly. Any time the Reds threatened to gather some momentum, the Dodgers quickly reaffirmed their dominance in this game.

Shohei Ohtani went 0 for 3 in his first game back with a couple of strikeouts and a walk. The good news is that the lineup didn't need him to win their fifth straight. Unlike Dreyer in the eighth, Evan Phillips had a clean ninth, securing his first save of the season.

Home runs— Teoscar Hernández (13), Eugenio Suárez (22), Elly De La Cruz (24)

WP— Emmet Sheehan (5-8): 5.2 IP, 3 hits, 1 earned run, 1 walk, 10 strikeouts

LP— Brandon Williamson (3-4): 4.1 IP, 3 hits, 6 runs, 3 earned runs, 5 walks, 4 strikeouts

SV—Evan Phillips (1): 1 IP, 2 strikeouts

It's the Dodgers' turn to deploy one of their aces on Tuesday (6:10 p.m. PT, SportsNet LA) as Tarik Skubal takes the ball, coming off his first start allowing double-digit hits in over two seasons—not that it particularly damaged his final line, allowing just two runs—with Nick Lodolo on the other side for the Reds.

articles.title: UTEP men’s basketball adds Youssouf Traore to 2026-27 roster
articles.summary: EL PASO, Texas (KTSM) — UTEP men’s basketball has added another significant piece to its roster, bringing in international standout Youssouf Traore. Head coa...
articles.body:
EL PASO, Texas (KTSM) — UTEP men's basketball has added another significant piece to its roster, bringing in international standout Youssouf Traore.

Head coach Joe Golding announced Sunday that Traore has signed with the Miners.

The 6-foot-10 forward arrives at UTEP after spending time playing professional basketball in Spain with Casademont Zaragoza in Liga Endesa, one of Europe's top domestic leagues.

Traore also brings extensive international experience with Mali.

He made a name for himself at the 2024 U18 AfroBasket tournament, earning MVP honors while helping Mali capture the championship. Traore averaged 12.8 points and 16.2 rebounds per game during the tournament, along with 2.7 assists.

He recorded a double-double in every game of Mali's championship run, including 15 points and 14 rebounds in the title-clinching victory over Cameroon.

Traore continued to make an impact on the international stage the following year.

At the 2025 FIBA U19 Basketball World Cup in Switzerland, Traore led Mali in scoring, rebounding and assists, averaging 17.1 points, 9.3 rebounds and 2.6 assists per game. He shot 57.5% from the field and recorded four double-doubles in seven games.

His best performance came against Argentina, when he scored 27 points and grabbed 12 rebounds.

Traore has also spent time in Spain, including with Casademont Zaragoza during the 2023-24 and 2025-26 seasons.

Now, he will bring that experience to UTEP as the Miners prepare for their first season in the Mountain West.

Golding said Traore's combination of size, length and athleticism was a major reason UTEP pursued him, particularly this late in the recruiting process.

"We are ecstatic to be able to bring Youssouf Traore to UTEP, especially this late in the process," Golding said. "He brings an element to the game that we need."

Golding added that Traore's experience playing overseas and for Mali's national teams should translate well to UTEP's new conference.

"His size, length and athleticism should all translate very well to the Mountain West Conference," Golding said.

Traore becomes the latest addition to a UTEP roster undergoing a significant overhaul heading into the 2026-27 season.

articles.title: Shay Whitcomb chops a single in 11th for 1st career game-ending RBI as Giants beat Cardinals 5-4
articles.summary: Shay Whitcomb chopped a single with one out in the 11th inning for his first career game-ending RBI, and the San Francisco Giants beat the St. Louis Cardinal...
articles.body:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Shay Whitcomb chopped a single with one out in the 11th inning for his first career game-ending RBI, and the San Francisco Giants beat the St. Louis Cardinals 5-4 on Monday night.

Drew Cavanaugh's sacrifice bunt against George Soriano (6-4) advanced automatic runner Nate Furman and put him in position to score the deciding run.

Jason Foley (3-1) pitched two innings for the win.

Bryce Eldridge tied the game at 4 on a single in the bottom of the 10th after St. Louis went ahead in the top of the inning when Leo Bernal's fly ball dropped in front of diving center fielder Jung Hoo Lee for a base hit.

Pinch-hitter José Fermín hit a tying sacrifice fly in the ninth for St. Louis against Giants closer Dylan Smith, who allowed a leadoff single to Joshua Báez and another base hit to Thomas Saggese before a one-out walk by Bryan Torres loaded the bases for Fermín.

articles.title: Cardinals Suffer Frustrating Loss on Infield Chopper, Fall Five Games Out of Playoff Race
articles.summary: Down 3-0 early in the game, the Cardinals rallied and got the game tied in the ninth inning on a sacrifice fly by Jose Fermin, and they took their first lead...
articles.body:
Roundtable Sports' John Denton breaks down the Cardinals' 5-4 loss to the Giants in 11 innings on Monday night -- a game where St. Louis went just 2 of 12 with runners in scoring position.

Maybe for the first time in his 47 years, Tony Vitello actuallyhoped that the St. Louis Cardinals lost a baseball game on Monday night. Unlikemost of the close games in his first rocky MLB season as manager of the San FranciscoGiants, Vitello came out a winner this time around.

Vitello, a native of St. Louis who grew up idolizing Ozzie Smith and rooting on the Cardinals, faced off against his boyhood team for the first time on Monday night and saw his Giants come through in the 11th inning for a rare victory in a one-run game.

After the Cardinals failed to score with runners at second and third in the top of the 11th, the Giants moved extra runner Nate Furman to third with a sacrifice bunt and scored him on an infield chopper by Shay Whitcomb for a 5-4 victory at Oracle Park.

The Cardinals (72-73) fell five games behind the Arizona Diamondbacks for the final Wild Card spot in the National League playoff chase. Arizona also holds the tiebreaker over the Cardinals by virtue of its 5-2 record in the head-to-head meetings.

The Cardinals moved extra runner Joshua Baez to third in the top of the 11th, but they failed to score when Nathan Church tapped out and Jose Fermin grounded out to shortstop. Church had an RBI double earlier in the game, and Fermin knotted the score at 3 in the ninth inning on a clutch sacrifice fly.

Cardinals' rookie catcher Leo Bernal delivered run-scoring single in the top of the 10th inning to give his team its first lead of the night. Then, after the Giants had tied the game against closer Riley O'Brien in the bottom of the inning, Bernal made a heads up play by bouncing out from behind home plate to field Drew Gilbert's ground ball while touching the plate and firing the ball to first for a double play to get the Cards out of a bases loaded jam.

The Cardinals (73-72) fell behind 3-0 before mounting severallate rallies and putting pressure on a Vitello-led Giants team that came into the nightwith MLB's worst record in one-run games (12-25).

Alec Burleson smoked a 431-foot homer that left the bat at109.5 mph in the sixth inning and Church doubled in another run in theseventh inning.

The Cardinals put the potential tying run in scoring positionin the seventh and eighth innings, before finally breaking through in the ninth to get the game tied. After Baez and Thomas Saggese reached on infieldsingles to open the ninth inning, Church's attempt for a sacrifice bunt waslined to Whitcomb at third base. Bryan Torres walked to load the bases and Fermin followed by drilling a high pitch into the outfield for the game-tying sacrifice fly.

In the bottom of the ninth, veteran reliever Ryne Stanek had to work out of a tense jam after loading the bases with two singles and a walk.

The Cardinals had no success against veteran right-hander BrandonWebb in the early going as he allowed just two singles and a walk over the game'sfirst five innings. Webb ended the first and second innings with strikeouts ofJordan Walker and Baez and he struck out Burleson, Walker and Lo Bernal in thefourth inning.

The Cards' first solid swing against the sinker-ballspecialist came in the sixth inning when Burleson turned on a letter-highsinker and smashed it 431 feet and into McCovey Cove beyond the right fieldseats. The homer was Burleson's 22nd on the season and it pushed hisRBI total to a career-best 104.

The Giants gave Webb a lead two batters into the game whenTurner Hill led off the bottom of the first inning with a walk and the red-hotDevers doubled high off the wall in right field.

San Francisco made it 2-0 in the third inning when theusually calm and cool McGreevy panicked on a liner hit back at him. When ChristianKoss' liner hit off McGreevy's glove, the pitcher bobbled it twice and triedflipping the ball to first base only to throw it high over Burleson's head foran error. Three batters later, Koss came around to score on a sacrifice fly byBryce Eldridge.

McGreevy, who limited the Giants to two earned runs and six hits while pitching 6 2/3 innings, made up for his earlier error with a dazzling bare-handed play to retire Osleivis Basabe to open the fourth inning.

Devers and Eldridge were in the middle of the next rallywith them smashing back-to-back doubles in the fifth inning to push SanFrancisco's lead to 3-0. Devers became the seventh player in the storiedhistory of the Giants to have 35 homers and 35 doubles in the same season.

After Monday's practice for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Sean Tucker's status for the season opener against the Cincinnati Bengals seems in question. Tucker was not a participant in Monday's drills, and the team could look to promote Josh Williams from the practice squad to take his place on the roster. The nature of the injury is undisclosed Bowles spoke to the media after training.

He said, "He's still rehabbing and he'll be a game-time decision right now."

Tucker made the 53-man roster as the third running back behind Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell. However, Tucker routinely showcases his ability around the goal-line and as a change-of-pace option for the Buccaneers. Williams did push for a roster spot over Tucker during training camp and preseason. Both have familiarity with the Buccaneers system.

When Tucker entered the NFL Draft in 2023, many respected his college production profile. He tabulated 3798 scrimmage yards and 31 total touchdowns at Syracuse. The expectation remained among fans that he would be one of the highest drafted running backs. However, a heart issue prevented Tucker from receiving that draft capital, and he went undrafted as a result.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers Sean Tucker Questionable Against the Cincinnati Bengals

Perhaps to the surprise of many, Tucker has a minimal injury history in the NFL. His heart condition has not seemed to be an issue. Throughout his career thus far, Tucker has accumulated 803 scrimmage yards and 11 touchdowns on 170 total touches. His efficiency at times remains impressive, but the Buccaneers protect him by using him sparingly.

Last season against the Buffalo Bills , Tucker ran for 106 yards on 19 carries with two touchdowns. When the Buccaneers call upon him, Tucker can provide a spark in a pinch. That being said, Irving and Gainwell are proven running backs, and it would take several injuries for Tucker to move up the depth chart. Not to mention, Williams also almost took Tucker's place on the 53-man, so his status cannot be guaranteed if this injury persists either.

Josh Williams Showcases a Similar Skillset to Tucker

Williams played running back at LSU for five years before declaring for the 2025 NFL Draft. He went undrafted, but the Buccaneers see something in him. This is the second straight season the team has kept him in the organization. In college, Williams produced for 2094 scrimmage yards with 18 touchdowns across five seasons. He was mainly a change-of-pace option, which is the role he challenges to take on the Buccaneers. If Tucker is unavailable, Williams could have an opportunity to solidify his case over Tucker on the roster.

Both running backs also offer versatility on special teams. Tucker has 41 kick returns for 1007 yards in his NFL career. Williams returned five kicks for 129 yards last season. Although, he only has four rushing attempts in the NFL, and will need to show more before given a significant workload.

articles.title: Nick Bosa will play against Rams in opener, defensive coordinator says
articles.summary: San Francisco 49ers defensive end Nick Bosa, sidelined since last September because of a torn ACL, will play in Thursday's season opener in Melbourne, defens...
articles.body:
MELBOURNE, Australia - The mystery is solved.

San Francisco 49ers defensive coordinator Raheem Morris told reporters ahead of Tuesday's practice at AAMI Park in Melbourne that defensive end Nick Bosa will play in the season-opener against the Los Angeles Rams .

"Oh, he's going out there," Morris said, after initially giving an unclear response and being asked to clarify in a follow-up question. "Whatever you want to say, he's going. He'll be there. We're not hiding that."

The announcement of Bosa's return ends more than a month-long saga since the 28-year-old began missing training camp practices. Bosa, who's coming off a torn right ACL, was dealing with lingering tendinitis from his recovery early in August.

Then, he suddenly returned for one practice last Wednesday, the morning of the 49ers' flight to Australia. After that practice, Bosa said his body felt great and that he was preparing to play.

"I'm just going to try and keep building, not get too up about it," Bosa said last Wednesday. "But it was a great day."

Yet Bosa wasn't present early on in Monday's practice, the 49ers' first one open to reporters in Melbourne. He was spotted in a video the 49ers' social media team posted of players entering the practice field. Bosa was sporting a baseball cap with his red jersey sleeves rolled up above his shoulders as he walked through the tunnel at AAMI Park.

"Nick Bosa is really easy," Morris said. "You watch this guy do it over a span, a long time in his career, been able to do it at different levels. … Bosa knows his body as well as anybody. He'll be prepared and ready to go as well as anybody."

A week ago, Bosa wasn't seen on the practice field Monday or Tuesday. He participated on Wednesday. It's possible that the Niners are using the same approach this week. But will Bosa be in game shape and ready to play against the Rams after participating in just one, or a small handful, of practices?

Fans were happy to see Shohei Ohtani return to the Los Angeles Dodgers ' lineup on Monday night, but he didn't contribute a single thing to their win.

The Dodgers put together some offense here and there, keeping the Cincinnati Reds in check to pick up a 6-3 win at UNIQLO Field at Dodger Stadium.

Ohtani went 0-for-3 with a walk and two strikeouts against Reds pitching. He now has a .277 batting average, something he probably wants to improve on before postseason play begins for the Dodgers.

After Cincinnati jumped out to a 1-0 lead in the top of the first inning, Los Angeles put up two runs in the bottom of the fifth, three runs in the bottom of the sixth, and a single run in the bottom of the eighth.

Teoscar Hernández appears to be showing up in style these days, which is good news for Dodgers manager Dave Roberts. Hernández, in the bottom of the sixth inning with Freddie Freeman and Max Muncy on base, smashed a three-run homer over the left-field wall. It was his 13th home run this season and gave Los Angeles a 5-1 lead at the time.

Hernández finished the game by going 2-for-3 at the plate with two runs scored and three RBIs.

Back in the bottom of the fifth inning, Alex Call was hit by a pitch and needed to come out of the ballgame. Hernández opened the inning with a single and stole his fourth base this season as Kyle Tucker 's struggles continued as he struck out. Hunter Feduccia also struck out before Call was hit by a pitch.

Miguel Rojas came on as a pinch hitter and reached first base on a wild throwing error from Reds third baseman Ke'Bryan Hayes. Hernández and Call scored on the errant throw and Rojas made it all the way around to third base.

Will Smith hit a bases-loaded sacrifice fly in the bottom of the eighth. Muncy scored and that wrapped up the Dodgers' offensive output.

Emmet Sheehan picked up the victory for the Dodgers, pushing his overall record this season to 5-8. Sheehan worked 5.2 innings, giving up three hits, one earned run, one walk, struck out a career-high 10 batters, and gave up one home run.

Evan Phillips came on in the ninth inning, recorded two strikeouts, and earned his first save this season. Five Dodgers pitchers in total were used by Roberts and, for Monday night, the bullpen held its own against Cincinnati.

When he's healthy, San Francisco 49ers star pass rusher Nick Bosa is one of the best pass rushers in the entire league. And despite questions about his health, it sounds like he'll be ready to go for the team's season opener.

Bosa tore his ACL last season and has been recovering ever since. While he may not be back to 100 percent just yet, it sounds like he'll be on the field.

During a game against the Arizona Cardinals on Sept. 21 of 2025, Bosa tore his ACL and underwent surgery just a few days later. That recovery, however, has not exactly gone according to plan.

As Bosa was coming back from his injury over the summer, he experienced a bit of a setback with soreness and tendinitis in his right knee, leading the 49ers to shut him down until Sept. 2, when he returned to practice.

All of that has led to some concern about whether or not he will be ready when the team takes the field in Australia this week, but it sounds like he's going to be there.

During a press conference this week, San Francisco 49ers defensive coordinator Raheem Morris announced that Bosa would indeed be able to play for the Niners when they open the season against the Los Angeles Rams this week.

"Oh, he's going out there. Whatever you want to say, he's going. He'll be there. We're not hiding that," Morris said, via Harrison Rich of the San Francisco Chronicle.

He might not be at 100 percent, but it's pretty clear that he will indeed be on the field for the team as they take on the Super Bowl favorites to open the season.

articles.title: Virginia Tech football: James Franklin has a message on Old Dominion Week
articles.summary: James Franklin downplayed it, but ODU has the Hokies’ full attention.
articles.body:
Two days after defeating the VMI Keydets 73-3, Virginia Tech head coach James Franklin met with the media on Monday. No more looking back. Well, Franklin did want to mention that he was not happy with his team's 11 penalties for 93 yards. Despite the 70-point win, Franklin stressed that this kind of undiscipline will come back to haunt the Hokies if they don't clean it up.

Then, Franklin turned his attention to this week's game, as Old Dominion returns to Blacksburg. Franklin noted history with ODU's coach, Ricky Rahne. Rahne first worked under Franklin in 2006 at Kansas State, when Franklin was the offensive coordinator. That partnership continued at Vanderbilt, where Brent Pry was also on staff, and stayed with him through the 2019 season, when he spent his final two seasons at Penn State as offensive coordinator.

Rahne has been ODU's head coach since 2020 and has faced Virginia Tech four times, going 2-2 against the Hokies, including last season's 45-26 win at Lane Stadium. That was the game that got Pry fired as head coach.

Franklin addressed his history with Rahne on Monday.

"Obviously, there's a ton of history between me and their head coach Ricky Rahne," Franklin said. "Our families are close, personally and professionally. Got a ton of respect for him and what he's been able to do at Old Dominion. Obviously, he's going to bring a team in here and a program, an organization that's going to be confident. They're going to come into Lane Stadium with confidence. They've won at home and on the road. So, as an organization, we're going to play a confident team."

Franklin noted that many others on Rahne's staff have worked with him before, but with this being game week, all those relationships go to the side for a few days.

Franklin was asked if last year's game added any fuel to this week's matchup. He downplayed it, adding that he's aware, his team is aware, and the Monarchs have their full attention.

"We'll watch last year's tape and be aware of it, but no, I don't think we're going to need to offer things like that as fuel," Franklin said. "But I think the reality is they already have our attention. 2-2 over the last four years is accurate, and the last time we played them was not just a loss, but a convincing loss. So, I wouldn't think I'm going to have to do anything from a fuel perspective; they've earned that. Old Dominion has earned that. So, I think they'll have our guys' attention. I think we're going to have to do any bulletin-board material, any of those types of things. We'll have the Norfolk State game on loop in our facility. We'll also have the game from last year on loop in our facilities."

Franklin explained why last year's game would be on loop at the facility. But, in reality, it's his way of motivating his team. For the players on last year's team, for Pry, that was embarrassing. Franklin would be crazy not to plant reminders.

If you're confident in one thing this weekend, you should be confident that the Hokies will not come out flat against ODU this time around.

articles.title: Patrick Mahomes faces ACL injury warning as his father encounters new hurdle over Chiefs games
articles.summary: Patrick Mahomes is facing an early warning over his ACL recovery ahead of the Kansas City Chiefs’ season opener, while his father has asked a judge for permi...
articles.body:
Patrick Mahomes is facing an early warning over his ACL recovery ahead of the Kansas City Chiefs' season opener, while his father has asked a judge for permission to travel to several games during the 2026 NFL season.

Mahomes is expected to start against the Denver Broncos in Week 1, just nine months after tearing his ACL. That has raised questions over whether the quarterback is returning too quickly.

There are also concerns about the protection Mahomes will receive, particularly with left tackle Josh Simmons potentially missing time while dealing with a lingering back injury.

Simmons' technique could put Mahomes at risk after dad deals with own situation

The biggest concern is not simply whether Mahomes is ready to return. It is also what could happen once he is back behind the Chiefs' offensive line.

Danny Heifetz of The Ringer Fantasy Football Show raised the possibility of Mahomes suffering another ACL injury because of Simmons' blocking technique.

"I think Patrick Mahomes is gonna tear his ACL again," Heifetz said.

He went on to explain that Simmons regularly uses a technique known as the "snatch technique", which involves grabbing a defender by the shoulder pads and throwing them down.

That could create a problem for Mahomes because Simmons could potentially send a defender towards his quarterback's legs.

Former Chiefs offensive tackle Mitchell Schwartz has also repeatedly criticised Simmons' use of the technique, particularly with Mahomes expected to have less mobility following his ACL injury.

Mahomes could also be asked to do plenty of work himself. Last season, he had to scramble frequently to help compensate for an explosive running game and pass-catching group that did not provide enough support.

Meanwhile, Patrick Mahomes Sr. is dealing with his own situation away from the field.

The quarterback's father is currently on probation in Texas after pleading guilty to his third DWI charge and has asked the court for permission to travel to Kansas City, Las Vegas and Cincinnati for Chiefs games.

According to court documents, Mahomes Sr. would still be required to complete urinalysis testing before and after each trip.

For the Chiefs, however, the immediate focus is on keeping their star quarterback healthy.

Mahomes' return comes with plenty of expectation, but the protection around him could prove just as important as his own recovery.

articles.title: Traverse City Horse Shows bring Olympians to Michigan, dollars to area
articles.summary: Three hours from Detroit is a 12-week horse show that brings Olympians and young equestrians to compete, then enjoy the summer life in Traverse City.
articles.body:
WILLIAMSBURG — Claire Francis returned to the barn beaming from her trail ride with her horse Rolland on the grounds of Flintfields Horse Park, the home of Traverse City Horse Shows .

A nice lady had agreed to ride with 13-year-old Claire after Rolland got nervous that they were alone on a hillside trail.

Claire, a Bloomfield Hills resident, had no idea the nice lady who rode with her, and gave her an oral history of the showgrounds in the process, was an Olympian.

"Margie Gold-something," Claire said later, trying to recall her new friend's name.

"Margie Gold-something" is Margie Goldstein Engle, one of the most accomplished equestrian show jumpers in United States history, and a trailblazer for women in the sport. Engle, now 68, has won over 250 Grand Prixs, the highest caliber of classes. She represented the United States in the 2000 Sydney Olympics and came in second in the World Equestrian Games.

That's the beauty of the Traverse City Horse Shows — a girl from the Detroit area can go for a trail ride next to a legend.

It's also a place where Michiganders who know nothing about horses can come watch amateur and professional riders compete up to an Olympic level in the hunter-jumper discipline of equestrian sports, winning prize money in the hundreds of thousands of dollars per class.

Most big horse shows in the country, like those in Kentucky and Florida, date back 50 or more years. In the last decade, Traverse City Horse Shows has grown from a four-week regional summer event to a 12-week international destination, attracting riders from across the world seeking top prize money and competition, but also a taste of summer life in Michigan.

They come for the show, rent houses and apartments on the Grand Traverse Bay, and spend their summers competing, boating and dining at Traverse City's array of restaurants.

The growth of the show in such a short time span has been part of a shift in the show jumping world from a traveling circus that picked up and went to a different regional show every week over the summer, to a one-stop shop of intense competition and lakeside life.

It has also been an economic boon to local communities in Williamsburg and Acme townships, Traverse City and Grand Traverse County.

In 2021, the show had an estimated local direct economic impact on the region of over $120 million, according to a study the show commissioned. The total economic spending on the show itself and in the region was about $350 million, the study determined.

The show took off during the COVID-19 pandemic, leaning into the advantages of an outdoor sport that already had social distancing baked in. It has also leaned on word-of-mouth in the everybody-knows-everybody world of top show jumping.

The show culminates Sept. 20 with its biggest class of the year, the $340,000 Longines Fédération Equestre Internationale Jumping World Cup. The class will bring at least nine of the world's top 30 riders to Michigan to end the summer, including U.S. Olympic silver medalists Kent Farrington and Karl Cook, ranked Nos. 1 and 24 in the world, respectively.

And yet, beyond seeing riders in their breeches at Meijer, many in the area and throughout Michigan still barely know the show exists, and some who do are not thrilled with how insular it is.

130 acres, 15 rings and up to 2,000 horses

Traverse City's horse show sits on 130 acres of land in a rural township about 20 minutes from the city.

Driving down Bates Road, just north of Route 72 and about two miles from the Turtle Creek Casino, a passerby would barely know the horse park is there. Only the gravel entrance with a gazebo and the backs of barns and tents are visible from the street.

But down the gravel driveway, the view opens up to seven pristine competition rings and seven practice rings, eight permanent barns and enough stalls for almost 2,000 horses.

There's dust, dirt and mud, but also immaculately cut grass, show rings with perfectly dragged footing, and elaborate show jumps painted bright colors with anything from giant sunflowers to swans attached.

In the early morning, the warm-up rings are full of riders and horses, all passing each other while walking, trotting and cantering in what looks like choreographed chaos as they work their horses ahead of the day.

Later, those same rings fill with riders in tailored coats and breeches, horses with tightly braided manes and bonnets over their ears, popping over white wooden jumps of varying heights as they prepare for the show ring.

During a class, one rider at a time steers their horse over a combination of obstacles, some 2 or 3 feet tall for the more intermediate-level riders, and others towering above 5 feet for the advanced and professional equestrian.

Farmland became home to a 'destination horse show'

Just two decades ago, those 130 acres were farmland until they were sold to a woman named Karin Flint.

Flint was on the board for the Motor City Horse Show, Detroit's biggest showjumping event. Founded in 1934, it ran until 2000 at the Bloomfield Open Hunt, when the club had to sell much of the land that held the show.

That brought an end to Detroit's show, and the region couldn't start another because a rule required top-rated shows to be at least 250 miles from another show. The Motor City show had been around long enough that it didn't matter, but any new show had to be far north to stay in Michigan because of an existing show in northern Indiana.

"I said, well why don't we go up north and see if anyone wants to come up?" Flint said in a phone interview with The News.

She partnered with show managers Dean and Alex Reinheimer to run a new show for Michigan, this time in Chums Corner, an unincorporated area in Grand Traverse County. A few years later, Flint bought the farmland in Williamsburg where the show now sits, and it became Flintfields Horse Park.

Flint said the show was family-friendly, including a playground, a bonfire night where everyone brought food to grill, and live music shows.

Dean Reinheimer said the vision was for a "destination horse show."

"I wanted to only have enough stuff to show 'til 5, and then I wanted to be done," he said. "Then people had five hours of lake time."

The first year, the riders were mostly from Michigan. Over a few years, it started attracting higher-level riders who were traveling from show to show across the Midwest during the summer. Many were based in Florida or California, seeking milder weather for themselves and their horses.

But families also saw the benefit, he said. They could take their kids salmon fishing, golfing, boating on days when there was no horse show.

Flint said the show started to grow beyond what she felt they could manage.

"That's kind of why I let it go, because I had a feeling it wanted to get bigger," she said.

Flint is still in the horse world — she owns the horse that just won a world championship last month in Para Dressage, for riders with disabilities. But she said she's proud of what came of the small, boutique-type horse show she started in Michigan.

"I watched all the kids grow up, and now they're all jumping Grand Prixs," she said.

Morrissey family takes over the Traverse City Horse Shows

When he received a call in 2015 about the opportunity to run a horse show in Michigan, Matt Morrissey had never been to Traverse City.

But the Cleveland-based Morrissey family had a long history of horse show management. His great-uncle founded Cleveland's horse show, which brought the first Grand Prix to North America in 1965.

Morrissey, 46, who runs the show with his father, Michael Morrissey, saw the same potential to make the Traverse City show a destination for riders and families.

"When you think about other shows around the country, they're in the middle of nowhere, most of them," he said. "So you have the horse show but nothing else really to do. This is the perfect family vacation for a family that has one or two kids that ride and other kids that don't."

For the first five years, the Morrisseys ran the horse show and had a lease-to-own option on the property. They purchased it outright in 2019, allowing them to start making major investments into the property — the kind that would attract top talent, including permanent barns instead of tents, expanded VIP areas, and top footing. Yes, the quality of the dirt matters for show rings.

Word started to spread that riders no longer had to go from show to show every week to compete against top talent. They could just come to Michigan and stay for a while.

The show grew to five weeks, then six, bringing in more prize money, which brought in more riders, which allowed for bigger prizes, more sponsorships and more investments in infrastructure.

They had no idea their biggest catalyst would be a pandemic.

It's not easy to ride a horse within 6 feet of another person.

So when the COVID-19 pandemic shut down just about everything across the country and in Michigan, the Morrisseys thought they had a good case for keeping a horse show going.

"Did we wrestle with it? Absolutely," Morrissey said.

But with the help of lobbyists and the top names in the equestrian world, the show was able to help urge Gov. Gretchen Whitmer to allow outdoor recreation events to be held, minus spectators, through the summer of 2020.

They were one of the only shows to open across the country, so the Morrisseys saw an opportunity. They created a 12-week schedule for the show, starting around July.

Riders came from all across the country, as Traverse City became their only option to compete during the pandemic summer. Many of them, Morrissey said, have kept coming back since.

"It was the start of all of our growth here," he said.

Morrissey said they put several protocols in place, including wearing masks even outside, limiting places to gather and keeping everything open-air.

Morrissey said the success that year and in 2021 "surprised us."

"We had the goal and the hopes of building this equestrian community, not just the show but the surrounding area, people committing to this area," he said. "But we didn't think it would happen this quickly."

Margie Goldstein Engle spent her career traveling across the United States and Europe showing horses at the top level. YouTube is full of old videos of her pulling off daring feats, like clearing a 7-foot jump . Her lifetime winnings total over $4 million.

But when she found Traverse City, she started setting up camp. It was more cost-effective and easier on everyone not to travel so much. She brought two horses this year, Jack and Dicas.

"To be able to go someplace and rent a house and be in at least a semi-normal environment, it's nice to be in one place for a little bit," Engle said in an interview from the fairgrounds in late July. "And it's nice the horses don't have to ship around quite so much."

A Miami native, Engle spends her winters in Wellington, Florida, arguably the horse capital of the U.S. But she and her husband, veterinarian Steve Engle, now spend the warmer months in Traverse City.

"It feels kind of like a summer home to us now," she said.

She's become an icon of the show, her rounds drawing rapt silence from the crowd and then an eruption of cheers when she rides well.

The Morrisseys also have a reputation for running a tight ship, Engle said. That attracts top talent.

"They know they're going to come here and it's going to be good footing and it's going to be run properly and they'll have good course designers, good jumps, (and will be) run efficiently," Engle said.

Olympians and Grand Prix riders find reasons to come to Traverse City

Erynn Ballard, currently ranked 30th in the world and a member of Canada's 2024 Paris Olympic team, is a frequent face and name at the showgrounds.

Ballard said she and her business partner brought about 60 horses to the show this year to ride and sell.

She said it's the perfect place to develop younger horses and riders, with so many different classes offered throughout the summer.

"If I travel around the world and I just go to the biggest horse shows, then the rest of it suffers a little bit," Ballard said. "And honestly, this is what I love."

During an early August Saturday Grand Prix, Ballard and Engle were both bested by a rider from Dusseldorf, Germany, just in town for the week, who planned to return in September after he got married.

Rupert Winkelmann could have stayed in Kentucky, where he usually spends his summers showing on the competitive circuit there. But he and his fiancée just like coming to Traverse City, and called it "built for horses."

"It's what we're looking for in a horse show," he said. "It ticks all the boxes."

Another draw, he noted, is the prize money. The class he won was worth $116,000, which is then split among the top finishers.

"For them to have such a prize purse the whole summer, it says a lot," he said.

Jen Markee, executive director of the North American Riders Group, said her organization rates various shows on the quality of their product, and Traverse City's always rates high. That's made it even more popular, she said, and some weeks, the show is now bursting at the seams with horses and riders.

The show has more work to do to accommodate the demand, she said, noting the top riders know which weeks not to come because of how busy it will be.

While the show itself takes up just 130 acres, its growth and popularity are beginning to impact the land around it.

Riders and trainers are starting to buy land around the show to have a home base in Traverse City to run their operations from Michigan during the summer.

Across the street from the show is a new development called Grand Prix Village. Top-level equestrians have bought plots of land to build barns, rings or grassy areas for horses to run.

A mile from the showgrounds, Angela Swanson and her husband recently purchased 80 acres that used to be a winery about a mile from the showgrounds.

Originally from Chicago, Swanson is now based in Florida for the winter but said they wanted to make Traverse City their summer home.

"It's a small town, but it's got great restaurants, it's got a great culture, there's a lot of different things to do, everybody's really friendly up here," she said.

Grand Traverse County Commissioner Darryl Nelson lives about half a mile from the entrance to the showgrounds. He's always loved being their neighbor, he said, although it was a few years before he came out to watch the show.

"It's just amazing," he said. "It was just an old farmstead, and now you feel like you're in Europe."

Nelson and his wife make money every summer renting their house out to riders and others associated with the show. He and his wife live in their RV on the property for about six weeks while his house is occupied.

Nelson also sits on the Cherry Capital Airport authority's board, and said the horse show has helped increase the number of direct flights to and from Traverse City.

The county, he said, has been able to give more tax breaks to developers to build new apartments or other projects in the region because of the money spent in the area over the summer.

"Not much of that money is from residents; it's people that are bringing that money in and spending it in our community," he said. "That's huge."

Nelson said some are unhappy to see the development in the area, which is not uncommon in rural areas near cities. Property values have risen in the area, which has made those looking to sell happy, he said. Locals looking to buy near the show, he said, might have a harder time.

Horse show 'feels like a lockout,' local realtor says

Still, not everyone said they feel the benefit from the influx of money from the horse show.

One realtor in town, Katy Bertodatto, said she regrets the show isn't more "collaborative" with the community.

"Whatever the reason, it feels like a lockout," she said. "... I know that the people up here would appreciate a more collaborative environment."

Bertodatto rents summer homes and said most of the horse show clients go through brokers associated with the show. The show feels insulated, both in its rural location and economic impact, she said.

"I would say the horse show kind of focuses on taking care of the horse show," she said.

Morrissey said they have a concierge on site during the show to aid with any needs, and have a few designated partners that have been vetted to help show attendees with things like housing. That started after a few attendees got scammed with rentals that weren't anything like what had been promised, he said, but they aren't exclusive deals. Attendees are free to book housing any way they prefer. The show also has an on-site campground, which books up early.

Morrissey said the show is committed to benefiting the community. The show is free to attend any day except for the Grand Prix, where admission is $15, and all the money goes toward a local charity. Each week is a different charity, and representatives come to accept a check in the ring during the show and promote their organization.

The show also sources as much of its labor and materials locally as possible, including wooden shavings for the bedding of horse stalls and hay, all from Michigan.

"To have that impact every year is something that the county, that northern Michigan can count on," Morrissey said.

Labor is harder, he said. They hire about 200 people every summer, but less than half are local. Many of the jobs at a horse show are specialized, including course designers, judges, farriers, and veterinarians, and have to be brought in from elsewhere. This year's course designer came from Germany.

Any food for sale at the show is from a local business, he said, including food trucks selling everything from coffee and lemonade to Mexican burritos.

The Traverse City horse show has not only brought Olympians to Michigan every year, but it's also given local riders a chance to show off their skills.

As an attorney with two young children, Traverse City resident Lauren Trible-Laucht always found time to ride horses, but rarely had a chance to show.

The Traverse City show gave her a way back into the ring.

"I'm just so spoiled that it's in my backyard," she said.

The 46-year-old now spends several weeks of the summer with her horse, Carerra Z, showing at Flintfields Horse Park. She is what's known as an "adult amateur" in the sport — someone in it just for fun.

On a typical day, Trible-Laucht will drive to the showgrounds in the morning, learn her course of jumps, help groom and tack her horse, and then climb into the saddle to warm up and show.

By 2 p.m., she's ready to head out to her kid's soccer practice.

"We're all just sort of having fun," said Trible-Laucht, who grew up in Rochester. "We know we're not going to the Olympics."

Trible-Laucht said this year was one of the first times her parents and other family came to the show. So many people who live in the area still don't know about the show or that they can come see it, she said.

"I think people are really surprised when they come up here, and they see the whole facility, and they see what it is," Trible-Laucht said.

Traverse City Pony Club president Cassandra Rossbach said she's lived in the area for 10 years and didn't know the show existed until her daughter started riding ponies a few years ago.

Now they bring the pony club kids to the show every year to see what they could do if they keep working on their riding — and to watch Olympians in their own town.

"You don't think of your little city, Traverse City, to bring in these international riders and international horses that are actually flown here," she said.

Riders from Metro Detroit are also finding their way up to Traverse City for the summer season.

Dori Dwan, an 11-year-old from Birmingham, rode her pony, Finn, in the show this summer, her second year there.

Last year, Dori said she got more nervous before each class. Now, she's more comfortable and helps the other new kids to the show get used to everything.

"It's really cool because you get to see really nice horses jump, and it's just really fun and they have really cool rings," Dori said.

Dori came to the show with her barn, Hillside Farm, which operates out of the Bloomfield Open Hunt with trainer Heather Irvine.

Irvine said she used to take students all across the country during the summer. Now they all drive three hours north and stay there for a week, a weekend or the full summer.

"Everybody's welcome," she said. "The thing that's great about this horse show is even if you're not real advanced, they have enough classes that you can get your feet wet, get started."

Engle's kind act 'epitomizes' Traverse City show experience, mother says

Claire Francis, the 13-year-old who rode the trails with Engle, also trains with Irvine. Irvine is a tough teacher, Claire said. But if she's feeling nice on a day off from the show, she'll take the kids tubing on her boat on the lake.

Claire said she loves coming to the show for the fun summer activities in addition to riding her horse.

"I love it so much," she said. "I love how it's outside… I love how there's fresh air everywhere, and I can take my dad there." Her dad is allergic to horses. Claire and Rolland were even crowned champions in their division one week this summer.

Her mother, Amy Francis, noted she's sometimes on thin ice with her daughter's school for pulling her out for horse shows.

But the lessons she has learned and the community she has built have been worth it, she said.

"Everybody's together up there, everybody cheers each other on," Francis said. "It's a great environment. Every penny spent in this sport is worth it to my husband and I. And I just love that, just watching her grow up there."

She said Engle taking in her daughter on a trail ride "really epitomizes the spirit of the show."

Claire was glad for the special opportunity to learn from a Show Jumping Hall of Fame inductee.

"I didn't know every single detail about the trail, and now I do," she said. "And I didn't know I met someone famous, and now I do."

articles.title: Zverev romps into quarter-finals as Darderi downed
articles.summary: Top seed Alexander Zverev romped into the quarter-finals of the US Open on Monday with a straight sets defeat of Italy's Luciano Darderi.Zverev, who had been...
articles.body:
Top seed Alexander Zverev romped into the quarter-finals of the US Open on Monday with a straight sets defeat of Italy's Luciano Darderi.

Zverev, who had been taken to five sets in his opening two matches of the tournament, raced past 21st seed Darderi 6-2, 6-2, 7-6 (7/3) in 2hr 30mins on the Arthur Ashe Stadium court.

The brisk victory came as a welcome change for Zverev, whose marathon first and second round matches had finished in the early hours of the morning.

"I don't know what to do with myself because it's before midnight," Zverev quipped afterwards. "I might go back to the practice court, I might go to a bar -- that was a joke, unfortunately.

"Compared to the first two matches, the level has been going up."

The 29-year-old French Open champion was in complete control throughout, punishing Darderi's woeful service game to grab an early double break in the first set for a 3-0 lead.

Darderi, who has failed to go further than the fourth round at any Grand Slam in his career, never looked like forcing his way back into the set thereafter.

Zverev mopped up the first set easily and was soon back on the attack in the second, once again securing a quick double-break for a 3-0 lead before holding with ease to go two sets up.

Darderi did manage to rally in the third set, suddenly finding his range with some blistering forehands and holding off four break points in the 11th game to help set up a tie-break.

But Zverev's superior service game meant there was only going to be one winner in the tie-break, a thunderous serve giving him a 5-2 lead before a scorching forehand into the corner took him to match point.

Zverev then wrapped up victory with his 13th ace of the match.

"I thought my level was very consistent," Zverev said.

"It was just he started playing incredibly well in the third set. I barely saw anyone hit the ball as hard consistently as he did in the third set," added the German, who will now face Dutch veteran Botic van de Zandschulp in the quarter-finals.

articles.title: Oklahoma Softball earns commitment from top-100 recruit in 2028 class
articles.summary: OU softball earns a commitment from in-state recruit Braylyn Saenz.
articles.body:
Oklahoma softball earned its first commitment in the 2028 class, and it's from an in-state talent.

​Braylyn "BP" Saenz announced her commitment to the Sooners on Monday night. Saenz is a four-star prospect out of Moore, Oklahoma, where she plays middle infield. But she can play all four infield positions. Saenz, who bats left-handed and throws right-handed, brings athleticism, a big arm, and power from the left side.

"First and foremost, I want to thank my Lord and Savior because without him none of this is possible," Saenze wrote in her commitment post. "I couldn't see him working through my journey at times, but he was in every part working it all together for his plan. I kept my faith and I kept working and I'm just so grateful and thankful."

She went on to thank her family and coaches.

Softball America rates Saenz as the No. 41 overall recruit, No. 13 at her position and No. 3 overall player in the state. Her commitment confirms OU head coach Patty Gasso's 'Go Boomer' post Monday evening.

Saenz announced her decision to commit to Oklahoma just a day after her visit this past weekend. She was one of four top-50 recruits who were in Norman. Saenz was joined by No. 1-ranked pitcher Sophia Schlader, No. 1 outfielder Caelyn Campos, and No. 22 overall player Gia Ryan. Before her visit over the weekend, where she watched the football team shut out UTEP 51-0, she took a camp visit on June 23.

After going undefeated in preseason , the Cincinnati Bengals are looking to keep the momentum going heading into the regular season .

The Bengals kick off their regular season with a Week 1 matchup in the jungle against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers . The regular season opener at Paycor Stadium is an Open in Orange theme , as the team will wear orange jerseys and white pants.

Here's everything you need to know to tune into Sunday's game.

Location: Paycor Stadium in downtown Cincinnati.

What channel is the Bengals-Bucs game on?

TV channel: FOX (WXIX-TV or Fox 19 in Cincinnati).

Streaming: Fubo, NFL+, NFL Sunday Ticket.

Listen: NFL+, Bengals Radio Network , WCKY-AM (1530), WEBN-FM (102.7), WLW700 and SiriusXM Ch. 88 .

articles.title: Patrick Mahomes’ Father in Wait-And-Watch Mode Over Court’s Permission To Attend Chiefs’ Games While on Probation for DWI
articles.summary: Pat Mahomes Sr. has asked a Texas judge for permission to travel outside the state to watch his son play for the Kansas City Chiefs, a reason familiar to foo...
articles.body:
Pat Mahomes Sr. has asked a Texas judge for permission to travel outside the state to watch his son play for the Kansas City Chiefs, a reason familiar to football parents everywhere. Mahomes Sr. is currently on probation following a 2024 DWI conviction.

According to court records reviewed by People and local station KLTV , the former MLB pitcher filed a motion on Friday, seeking approval to attend seven Chiefs games in Kansas City, Las Vegas and Cincinnati.

Patrick Mahomes Sr. Requests Travel Exception

People reported that the 56-year-old is "hoping the court will allow him" to make the trips during the 2026 season. Notably, the filing does not ask the court to remove his supervision requirements.

Instead, Mahomes Sr. acknowledged that he would remain subject to urinalysis testing requested by his supervision officer before and after each trip.

The motion also states that Mahomes Sr. has completed 160 hours of community service and a 16-week outpatient treatment program.

KLTV reported that a Smith County community supervision officer verified his compliance with his current probation conditions and that he continues to be monitored with an ankle device.

Earlier, Mahomes Sr. pled guilty in August 2024 to his third driving while intoxicated charge after a February arrest in Tyler, Texas. It was then reported that his blood alcohol content was 0.23 when he was pulled over.

BE THE GM OF YOUR FAVORITE TEAM: PFN's Free NFL Mock Draft Simulator

As a result, the court sentenced Mahomes Sr. to five years of probation, including one year of intense supervision. The legal situation became complicated as the authorities arrested him on Feb. 3 after alleging that he consumed alcohol in violation of his probation, according to Smith County District Attorney Jacob Putman.

KLTV reported that the court sentenced Mahomes' father to 30 days in jail, with credit for time served, and extended his probation by two years.

The travel request would allow Mahomes Sr. to attend seven games this season. No ruling on the motion was reported as of Sunday afternoon, so the request remains pending.

Mahomes Sr. spent 11 seasons in Major League Baseball from 1992 through 2003, including five years with the Minnesota Twins.

He also pitched for the Boston Red Sox, New York Mets, Texas Rangers, Chicago Cubs, and Pittsburgh Pirates before continuing his professional career outside the majors.

The family has spoken publicly before about the effect Mahomes Sr.'s legal troubles had on his QB son.

In ESPN's 2025 docuseries The Kingdom , both Mahomes and Mahomes Sr. discussed how the 2024 arrest forced the three-time Super Bowl champion to address questions about his father while preparing for Super Bowl LVIII.

For now, the latest development is procedural and does not guarantee Mahomes Sr. will be in the stands. Whether he gets to make those trips now depends on the Texas judge.
